title: Senior Liberal slams Blyth in email to members, saying ‘you gave her your trust, she threw it away’ – as it happened
description:
• Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Pauline Hanson has released a statement this morning welcoming South Australian senator Leah Blyth to her party.

Blyth is the second high-profile federal defection from the Coalition to One Nation – after Barnaby Joyce.

Senator Blyth will be One Nation’s first So
text: What we learned today, Thursday 26 November
We’re wrapping up the blog for the day. Thanks for reading. Here’s a reminder of our top stories:
Leah Blyth, a Liberal senator for South Australia, has defected to One Nation and will become the party’s first upper-house member for the state.
The Liberal shadow minister Anne Ruston has issued a scathing statement on Blyth’s move, claiming her fellow South Australian “put her own interests ahead of” voters.
The energy minister, Chris Bowen, has declared coal-fired power stations must be replaced, with the stations facing at least one breakdown every day for three years.
The federal government has forecast Australia will reduce its carbon emissions by 42% on 2005 levels by 2030 – just under its target for a 43% cut.
The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, says the uptick in unemployment last month was “a very bad development”, but defends the government.
Nicolette Boele, the Bradfield MP, has said Chris Bowen has not learned from the Cop31 focus on fossil fuels.

A Victorian Coalition government would privatise two sewage plants and sell off state-owned land, renewable energy assets and the “air rights” between Richmond train station and the Melbourne Cricket Ground if elected.
Joyce responds to ‘turncoat town’ taunt against One Nation
One Nation’s deputy leader, Barnaby Joyce, has responded to his former Nationals colleague Matt Canavan’s argument that his party is “turncoat town” by hoovering up defectors from other parties.
Canavan, the Nationals leader, made the comments this morning as he slammed Leah Blyth over her defection from the Liberal party to One Nation.
Joyce, who defected to One Nation last December, says he expected “this sort of screeching”:
double quotation markWhat are we going to say to all the voters who have changed too? Are they all turncoats? Thirty per cent of Australians, are they turncoats?
Joyce says people have followed their “political logic” and wanted “a greater representation of conservatism in politics”.
Blyth ‘has shown disloyalty to her leader, party and state’, Wilson says
The shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, says his former colleague Leah Blyth’s defection to One Nation is disloyal.
Blyth’s move blindsided Coalition MPs who branded her a “turncoat”, raising further scrutiny of chaos inside the opposition.
Wilson says he discovered the South Australian senator’s move by reading about it “in the newspaper like everyone else”:

double quotation markI actually just think it’s sad, to be honest. I think one of the things that conservatives value is loyalty. And we know that Barnaby Joyce, as an example, showed disloyalty to his leader, his party and his community. And now we’ve got Leah Blyth, who has shown disloyalty to her leader, party and state.
About half of Labor’s forecast savings lost in private health deal with Greens, Butler says

The health minister, Mark Butler, has appeared on the ABC where he is asked about the federal government striking a deal with the Greens to carve out all pensioners from its private health insurance rebate changes.
Butler acknowledges the government has lost about half of the $3bn forecast savings to get the legislation passed in the final sitting week of the year.
He says it is “unlikely” to be reconciled in next month’s mid-year budget update:
double quotation markWe need to reconcile that in a future budget update, of course. In the following budget update, which will be next May, we’ll have to have reconciled that.
Senior Liberal slams Blyth in email to party members
The Liberal shadow minister Anne Ruston has issued a scathing statement on former colleague Leah Blyth, claiming her fellow South Australian “put her own interests ahead of” voters.

Ruston, the senior Liberal from SA, said in an email to members that she was “incredibly disappointed” in Blyth’s defection to One Nation. She noted Blyth was “never elected to the Senate seat she holds”, and was instead appointed by the Liberals – the party she just quit – to fill a casual vacancy, and hadn’t faced the ballot box.
“You gave her your trust. Today she threw it away,” Ruston wrote to members.
“South Australians sent a Liberal to Canberra to fight for them. Today, Leah chose to put her own interests ahead of theirs.”
Thank you all so much for joining me on the blog this week, for the final sitting of the year.
I’ll leave you with the fabulous Adeshola Ore for the rest of the afternoon.
Tl;dr here’s what happened in question time
“It’s the economy, stupid,” was the Coalition’s MO today, trying to corner Anthony Albanese and Jim Chalmers on inflation, jobs and mortgage rates.
The pair tried to turn the attention back to the Coalition, taking every chance they could to taunt Angus Taylor on Leah Blyth’s defection to One Nation.

There were several bootings out of the chamber today: the Labor MP Rowan Holzberger, before QT even started, Nationals deputy leader, Darren Chester, and Liberal MP Simon Kennedy together, and Labor MP Matt Burnell.
Albanese fired up over a question from the independent MP Kate Chaney over a contentious defence bill that experts have warned could have serious human rights implications.
And independent Rebekha Sharkie asked the aged care minister about unspent funds – he said it was because the sector was slow to respond to additional funding.
Question time ends for the year but Burke announces Friday sitting for house
After a final dixer to the prime minister, Anthony Albanese calls time on QT for the year.
BUT … before everyone leaves, Tony Burke announces that the house will sit again tomorrow at 8am.
It won’t be a long morning, MPs will quickly vote through any legislation passed through the Senate with amendments later tonight.
Aged care minister asked about unspent budget funds

Back to the crossbench, Rebekha Sharkie asks the aged care minister, Sam Rae, why the government underspent on aged care by $1.4bn in the last financial year, when “more than 190,000 older Australians remain waiting for an assessment or Support at Home, and last year over 6,400 older Australians died while waiting for their approved aged care.

Rae has a long preamble and says Labor has “effectively doubled the size of the aged care budget” since it came to government and that by the end of this financial year, “this homecare system will have tripled in size since 2020”.
He then gets to the meat of the question.
He says the money unspent is a small proportion of the total budget (which this financial year will be $44bn) and was largely due to the sector responding to investing in the sector at a “slow rate”.

double quotation markThe money to which the member’s question pertains, that was not spent through that period, was obviously, as a proportion, a relatively modest part of that, but had to do with the slower rate at which the sector has been able to respond to investments both in the residential space, through challenges in construction particularly, of new residential aged care facilities, as well as the Support at Home system and the rapid increase of places, the workforce challenges making it difficult to respond.
Chalmers says unemployment rise a 'very bad development'

Back to the opposition, the Liberal MP Henry Pike says last month, 43,000 Australians lost their jobs and asks the treasurer, how many Australians are “at risk of losing their job and losing their home?”
Jim Chalmers says the uptick in unemployment last month was “a very bad development”, but defends the government, saying:
double quotation markWe ask those opposite to acknowledge that what we’ve seen under this government is the lowest average unemployment of any government in the last 50 years.
On house prices, he still says they are up about 15% over the past five years.

double quotation markEven in the context of some serious challenges – inflation, productivity, global volatility – a tick-up in the unemployment rate, what we’ve been reminded of this week, whether it’s dwelling investment or business investment more broadly today, is that we do have a lot coming at us, but we’ve got a lot going for us as well. And if those opposite really cared about confidence in our economy, they’d stop talking the place down.
‘Conspiracy theories and misinformation’: Albanese frustrated by defence bill concerns
Anthony Albanese has fired up over a question by the independent MP Kate Chaney about scrutiny over a controversial defence bill, angrily branding criticisms as “nonsense” and misinformation.
For a recap on the bill, see here:

Chaney says that bill, which “allows ministers to set aside commonwealth, state and territory laws, sometimes without publication, and to declare security zones where failing to follow criminal directions is an offence”, passed with limited parliamentary scrutiny and little time for public submissions. She asks what the minimum amount of scrutiny for such a consequential bill should be.
Albanese quickly starts shouting at Chaney, irritated by the question:

double quotation markI have seen some nonsense on social media – not from the member for Curtin, but from others – that simply feeds conspiracy theories that don’t just come from the far right, but can come from the far left as well. And what this legislation is about is simply making sure that our defence institutions and infrastructure are kept safe. And quite frankly, to suggest that a minister would abuse powers in order to designate something that was not associated with defence of this country as somehow needing protection is quite frankly irresponsible, and those spreading that misinformation online should know better.
Chaney tries to make a point of order, saying the question was about minimum scrutiny.
The Labor MP Matt Burnell shouts out, “don’t want to keep Australians safe”, and promptly gets kicked out of the chamber.
Treasury and RBA not forecasting recession, Chalmers says

Staying on the economy, the Nationals MP David Batt says Gerry Harvey, the chair of major retailer Harvey Norman, has warned recession is inevitable and asks the treasurer if he will “guarantee Australia will not go into recession”.
The Labor benches laugh as Batt mentions Harvey, forcing him to ask the question twice.

Harvey has previously been critical of Labor and was criticised for repaying just $6m of the $22m in jobkeeper payments Harvey Norman received during Covid, after it posted record profits in the 2020-21 financial year.
Jim Chalmers says more seriously that he respects Harvey, but tries to stick it to the Coalition, accusing the opposition of wanting the economy to fail, to score a political win.

double quotation markWhen it comes to the prediction that [Harvey] has made – and there are a range of predictions, a range of opinions – all I can say … is that neither the Treasury nor the Reserve Bank forecasts have the Australian economy going backwards. I know that’s a matter of great disappointment to those opposite, because those opposite desperately want the Australian economy to fail, because they see that as the only way that they might succeed.
‘Stop talking the Australian economy down’: Chalmers under pressure over inflation numbers

The shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, is next and asks if the prime minister, who yesterday said Australia’s inflation rate is at least better than the Philippines, can “identify a single major advanced economy with a higher core inflation rate than Australia?”
Jim Chalmers takes the question (cue groans from the Coalition benches) and says broadly, “inflation is going up around the world”.
double quotation markAround the world, I think every major advanced economy, from memory, has seen inflation go up in October.
But Chalmers won’t name any countries – other than the Philippines.
Wilson tries to bring Chalmers back on track, making a point of order on relevance, which Milton Dick isn’t having.
Chalmers goes for the jugular.
double quotation markI hear the leader of the opposition interjecting. He’s very mouthy for someone who lost a shadow minister, Mr Speaker. Stop talking the Australian economy down.
Chalmers defends budget: ‘I won’t be taking lectures on budget responsibility from those opposite’
The Nationals MP Jamie Chaffey doesn’t bother asking the government this time how much more mortgage holders are paying than when the Albanese government was first elected.

Chaffey says, after 17 interest rate rises, the average new mortgage holder is more than $30,000 a year worse off, and asks the treasurer to admit “he has broken the economy” and apologise to households.
Jim Chalmers says he acknowledges the extra pressure that interest rate rises put on households.

He then pivots, taking a shot at the Coalition, accusing opposition MPs of wanting to “talk about budget repair – they like to talk about responsible economic management. They just don’t like to vote for it.”

double quotation markYou know what they did when inflation was north of 6% and roaring? They had a net spend in their last budget of $40bn. And you know how many saves they had in that last budget, Mr Speaker? Absolutely none. So I won’t be taking lectures on budget responsibility from those opposite.
PM urges parliament to support gas reservation scheme
Over to the crossbench, the independent MP Dai Le asks the prime minister if he will support her bill to ensure 30% of goods in commonwealth projects are made in Australia.
The government rarely, if ever, supports crossbench bills.
Anthony Albanese says by that measure, Le should be a fan of the government’s Future Made in Australia program.
“No!” shout a bunch of Coalition MPs.
Albanese says Le and the Coalition should support the gas reservation scheme:

double quotation markOne of the reasons why we have had a domestic gas reservation for the east coast that hopefully will pass the Senate today is because of what that will do – make Australian manufacturing more competitive by making sure that there is a limit on the price of gas, which is absolutely critical for Australian manufacturing.
Two Coalition MPs kicked out
The government’s dixers have so far been used to talk up the gas reservation scheme and pressure the Coalition to support it.
So far, the Coalition have said they “will not oppose it”.
At the end of a dixer, Pat Conroy finishes his answer with this burn to the Liberals: “Time to get off the fence, otherwise you’re just going to get some splinters.”
Milton Dick then reckons it’s time to thin out the chamber a little. He kicks out deputy Nationals leader, Darren Chester, and Liberal frontbencher Simon Kennedy.
“Don’t look surprised,” Dick says.
Taylor ‘can’t even run his own frontbench’, Albanese says
Angus Taylor is back to the dispatch box with another tight question: “How much has the cost of the average annual mortgage payment gone up over the last four years?”
Spoiler alert: he won’t get a number.
Anthony Albanese says very broadly that house prices have risen more than 400% since the capital gains tax discount was introduced by the Howard government.
Taylor, obviously unhappy with the answer (or lack thereof) so far, gets up with a point of order and says:
double quotation markIt’s a very specific question – how much has the cost of the average annual mortgage payment gone up over the past year? I’ll give you a hint – it’s over $30,000 a year.
Milton Dick calls that an “abuse” of points of order.
double quotation markHe wants to run the country, but he can’t even run his own frontbench, Mr Speaker … We understand why he’s angry.
That’s too far for the manager of opposition business, Dan Tehan, who makes a point of order, and then another point of order when his first isn’t adhered to.
Albanese ends his question continuing his attacks.
Liberal members 'tossing up whether to leave or remain', PM says

The Coalition’s got its focus set on the economy again today, with Angus Taylor asking Anthony Albanese if he can “name a single economic indicator that has gone in the right direction this year”, with inflation and wages going backwards.
The prime minister says employment numbers and the gender pay gap are going in the right direction.

double quotation markThe employment rate – now, there is 14.7 million Australians employed. There were 13.5 million employed when we came to office. So that’s up … The gender pay gap is at a record low, 11.3%. It was 14.2% when we came to office.
He then also tries to take a crack at Leah Blyth’s defection. You can tell his office has spent some time trying to come up with different ways of sticking in the knife:

double quotation markPeople are looking at ways in which they could have growth. My friend Andy Burnham in the UK is looking at revisiting Brexit there. It looks like Liberal members are also tossing up whether to leave or remain.
Before questions even begin, Tony Burke takes the opportunity to have a crack at the Coalition over Leah Blyth’s defection.
Referencing a new frontbench “list” submitted by the Coalition to the house after the shadow home affairs minister Jonno Duniam’s resignation, Burke points out that it’s already out of date.

double quotation markWhen there’s a change in the government or the opposition executive, that the new list is tabled. The list that’s been tabled for the opposition includes someone who’s no longer even a member of the Coalition. And so the ordinary practice would be for an updated list to be tabled at the start of question time.
There’s plenty of shouting across the chamber and the Labor MP Rowan Holzberger has just been kicked out.
